transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Rodriguez (Orchid - Head of ML), Ethan Li (Orchid - Platform), Priya Shah (Orchid - Security)
Recording ID: ff-20260304-orchid-001

Summary: High-level discovery on Private deployment. Customer is exploring private VPC options: peering, PrivateLink/private endpoints, region residency, and KMS/HSM for key management. Wants minimal public egress, audit logs, and SLA for PII-sensitive inference.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Maya: yep, loud and clear.
[00:04] Ethan: good.
[00:06] Avery: cool, quick intros - i'm avery, i'm the account exec, and samir is our solutions engineer. we do these private VPC discovery calls usually to map out network constraints and security reqs.
[00:17] Samir: hi all, i'm samir. i'll be the technical lead on the redwood side for the pilot.
[00:21] Maya: maya here - head of ml at orchid. we're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private. our main concern is PHI handling and we need to keep traffic inside our aws accounts and regions where possible.
[00:33] Priya: priya, security. looking for SOC2, audit logs, kms integration, and enforcement of egress restrictions.
[00:40] Ethan: ethan, platform. i'll be owning networking and infra for the pilot.
[00:44] Avery: great. to start, can you run through your current infra and constraints? what vpc setup, accounts, and regions are we talking about?
[00:53] Maya: sure - most of our infra is in us-east-1, we also have workloads in eu-west-1 for EU customers. everything sensitive lives in the main production account, with a dedicated ML account for experimentation. we'd prefer the inference to sit in our prod account or a peered account; we don't want to route data over the public internet.
[01:10] Ethan: yeah we don't want any public endpoints. ideally private connectivity to the inference endpoints, and we need options for cross-account peering or AWS PrivateLink.
[01:19] Samir: okay that makes sense. two typical patterns we see: 1) VPC peering or Transit Gateway peering between your VPC and redwood-managed VPCs or 2) PrivateLink/private endpoints where redwood exposes a private endpoint into your VPC. each has tradeoffs.
[01:34] Avery: and then there's the fully private deployment option - redwood private - where we install the control plane into your VPC or run a customer-dedicated instance in your account. that avoids any external routing.
[01:45] Priya: what's the difference operationally between dedicated and private again? we've heard dedicated means reserved capacity but still managed by redwood - is traffic still going out?
[01:55] Samir: good question. dedicated is reserved GPU pools in redwood's cloud; network model can vary: for our hosted dedicated, traffic still terminates in our infra and you can use IP allowlists and private endpoints, but there is egress to the redwood environment. private (VPC/private deployment) runs in your VPC or under your account, so traffic stays within your network and keys and logs can remain under your control.
[02:16] Maya: ok we're leaning private mainly because of the compliance posture. can you explain the PrivateLink option - would that require us to accept an endpoint service from redwood? any limitations on regions?
[02:27] Samir: yes PrivateLink is implemented as an AWS endpoint service. you create an interface endpoint in your VPC which connects to our service. pros: you get private connectivity without peering, cross-account pathing is simpler. cons: it requires ENIs and IPs in your subnets; if you have many subnets or heavy throughput you need to plan IP capacity. PrivateLink is regional, so you'd need endpoints in each region (us-east-1, eu-west-1).
[02:47] Ethan: what about latency with PrivateLink vs peering vs local private deployment? we're very latency-sensitive - sub-100ms for inference is ideal.
[02:57] Samir: generally: local private deployment - best latency, lowest hop count; VPC peering/transit - similar, depends on routing and TGW; PrivateLink adds an extra network hop to the ENI and the NLB, slightly higher p99 but still acceptable in many cases. we've benchmarked p50/p95 in hosted setups; for strict SLA you'd want the private deployment in your account.
[03:17] Priya: for KMS, does redwood support customer managed keys (CMK) or HSM integration? we need to ensure key separation for any PII-backed models.
[03:26] Samir: we support customer-managed KMS keys for encryption at rest for model artifacts and logs. for private deployments we can integrate with your KMS; HSM integrations are possible via dedicated setups - we'll need legal and compliance signoff for HSM in some cases.
[03:38] Maya: audit logs - do we get full request/response logs? any redaction controls? retention options?
[03:45] Avery: we can provide detailed audit logs and request-level metadata. we do not store customer prompt text in plaintext for hosted unless configured; for private deployments you can choose to store logs in your own S3 with lifecycle rules. retention is configurable; we can surface logs to your SIEM via Kinesis or S3.
[03:59] Priya: perfect. also need SSO and RBAC, we're using Okta.
[04:05] Samir: we support SAML/Okta and role-based access. for private installs you can map roles to IAM as well.
[04:11] Ethan: back to networking: you mentioned Transit Gateway. could we connect via our existing TGW instead of peering to simplify many VPCs?
[04:19] Samir: yes Transit Gateway is a common pattern for customers with lots of VPCs. we can peer our VPC to your TGW or we can place the redwood-managed VPC behind your TGW in private deployments. routing considerations are important - route propagation and security controls need to be coordinated.
[04:33] Maya: what's the typical on-prem option? one of our clusters is air-gapped for very sensitive workloads.
[04:39] Avery: for air-gapped we offer an on-prem package where the inference runtime runs on your hardware and control plane is offline or connected via a relay. it's more involved - long lead time and legal.
[04:49] Priya: do you support VPC endpoints for S3 and other services used by the runtime? we need no egress to internet for model downloads.
[04:58] Samir: yes, the private deployment can be configured to use VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, KMS. model artifacts can be pulled from your S3 via VPC endpoints; we can support limited egress for updates under controlled channels if needed.
[05:10] Ethan: any constraints on region parity? we need inference in eu-west-1 for EU customers. can you run the private deployment there?
[05:18] Samir: we support deployments in most major commercial regions, including us-east-1 and eu-west-1. there may be capacity constraints for certain GPU types, but we can propose compatible instance types. for private within your account, it's entirely up to you where you deploy.
[05:31] Maya: capacity - if we need burst traffic for batch jobs, can the private deployment autoscale?
[05:36] Samir: yes we support autoscaling policies; depends on your capacity plan. for strict capacity guarantees we typically use Dedicated reserved pools or a hybrid: a private control plane with burst to redwood Dedicated. that hybrid requires explicit routing and escape hatches.
[05:51] Priya: that hybrid sounds like it has risk - external burst would cross accounts. is there a way to have a fallback but still keep data residency?
[05:58] Samir: we do automatic fallback policies that can route to lower-tier models or to redwood-hosted endpoints, but for PII-sensitive data we can disable cross-account fallback. it's a policy knob. we recommend explicit runbooks for fallbacks.
[06:12] Ethan: how are IPs and security groups handled for PrivateLink? we want to limit which subnets can reach the endpoint.
[06:19] Samir: PrivateLink uses interface endpoints so you can control via SGs and NACLs. for VPC peering you'd control via route tables and SGs. we provide suggested sg rules (TLS 443) and a small set of IP ranges for administrative access.
[06:33] Maya: do we need to open any non-TLS ports for KV cache or gRPC?
[06:38] Samir: typically TLS 443 is enough for API traffic. for metrics and tracing we can push to your endpoints over TLS. if you run the runtime in your cluster (private install) internal ports for the runtime may need to be opened, but we provide the list.
[06:51] Priya: compliance-wise, can we get a diagram of data flows and an SOC2 snapshot?
[06:56] Avery: yes, we'll send a security whitepaper, SOC2 report, and a redwood network diagram.
[07:02] Maya: what's the onboarding timeline if we go private? we're aiming for a pilot in 6 weeks. is that feasible?
[07:08] Samir: a basic private pilot in your account is usually 4-8 weeks depending on procurement and networking approvals. if you need on-prem air-gapped that's longer. 6 weeks is reasonable for a scoped pilot.
[07:18] Ethan: ok procurement question - does private deployment require long-term commitment? we prefer to trial before multi-month commitments.
[07:25] Avery: pilots can be short term; reserved capacity contracts apply only for dedicated commits. private deployments have licensing and support fees which we can make pilot-friendly. we'll include pricing options.
[07:35] Maya: can you run a short perf benchmark? we'll give a sample payload and expected concurrency.
[07:40] Samir: yes - action item: send a perf harness and instructions. we'll need expected qps, average token length, and concurrency.
[07:48] Priya: one more - logging: where do traces live? can we push to datadog?
[07:53] Samir: yes we integrate with datadog and you can ship traces to your own tracing endpoint. for private, we can push directly to your datadog account or write logs to your S3.
[08:03] Avery: quick recap of next steps - avery will send SOC2 and network security docs by friday, samir will draft a recommended network diagram and PrivateLink vs peering pros/cons, and maya/ethan will confirm regions and expected qps. we'll propose a pilot plan targeting 6 weeks.
[08:18] Maya: sounds good. thanks.
[08:20] Ethan: thanks all.
[08:21] Priya: thanks.
[08:22] Avery: we'll follow up with the artifacts. end recording.
